title: BridgeLane Redwood SDK & Auth Quickstart - Env Setup (Python/TS)
summary: Kickoff walkthrough of Redwood SDK quickstart for BridgeLane: auth patterns (API keys, SSO, KMS), environment setup for Python/TS, sandbox vs dedicated choices, and brief Optimize/batching recommendations. Agreed next step: sandbox invite + security docs and sample CI key rotation workflow; POC scoping meeting to follow.
topics: Sandbox vs Dedicated vs Private deployment
Security: SOC2, KMS, SSO, audit logs
transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-06-03 15:30 UTC | Duration ~48m | Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Carlos Rivera (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (BridgeLane), Evan Shaw (BridgeLane), Jordan Miles (BridgeLane)

[00:00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call?
[00:00:05] Priya Nair: Priya here, lead ML.
[00:00:07] Evan Shaw: Evan, platform.
[00:00:09] Jordan Miles: Jordan, dev lead.
[00:00:11] Maya Chen: Great. Our goal today is a hands-on quickstart for the Redwood SDKs — Python and TypeScript — and to cover auth and env setup so your CI/CD can call the hosted API without leaking keys. We'll also touch on Console and Optimize tips. Carlos will demo the code.
[00:00:28] Carlos Rivera: Hi all — I'll share my screen in a sec. We'll start with the simplest path: sandbox API key, local quickstart, then show how you'd swap to a dedicated token or VPC/private deployment later.
[00:00:41] Jordan Miles: Sounds good. Our main concerns are key rotation in CI, data residency, and predictable p99 latency.
[00:00:48] Maya Chen: Noted. Priya, can you remind us of your target throughput and latency SLOs for the PoC?
[00:00:55] Priya Nair: For the initial PoC, around 30 requests/sec, p95 < 600ms on short prompts. We'll evaluate cost and then scale.
[00:01:03] Carlos Rivera: Ok that maps fine to a small dedicated pool later. For now sandbox can emulate behavior, though absolute latency will differ.

[00:01:12] -- Demo start --
[00:01:14] Carlos Rivera: Alright, code. This is the python quickstart in the repo we shared. First step: pip install redwood-inference-sdk (note: our examples use "redwood" name in code comments, sometimes transcribed as "Redwood Dedkate" in older notes, ignore that).
[00:01:30] Carlos Rivera: Set env var REDWOOD_API_KEY locally or in your CI secret store. Example export REDWOOD_API_KEY=sk-xxxx. In CI we recommend vault or your cloud secrets manager and not checking keys into repo.
[00:01:44] Evan Shaw: For CI rotation, do you have a recommended TTL or rotation cadence?
[00:01:49] Maya Chen: We recommend short-lived keys backed by KMS/HSM where possible. For Hosted accounts you can generate scoped keys per environment and rotate every 30-90 days; for Dedicated/Private we integrate with customer KMS so rotation can be automatic. We'll share a sample GitHub Actions workflow.
[00:02:04] Priya Nair: Can you show the sample workflow?
[00:02:06] Carlos Rivera: Yep, here's a simple GH Actions step that pulls REDWOOD_API_KEY from secrets and calls a smoke test. We'll paste the snippet in the follow-up.

[00:02:20] [00:02:20] -- TypeScript quickstart --
[00:02:22] Carlos Rivera: TS example: npm install @redwood/inference (we had a couple naming inconsistencies in docs, the package is @redwood/inference). Use process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY in node or set up dotenv for local dev.
[00:02:37] Jordan Miles: For serverless functions, any size limits or cold-start concerns?
[00:02:41] Carlos Rivera: Calls are standard HTTP calls to our runtime. For serverless cold starts, the usual function warmup applies. For lower latency SLOs you can use Redwood Dedicated or pin to a hot pool; we have warm pool options and autoscaling policies.

[00:02:58] Maya Chen: Let's switch briefly to Console so you can see the token and sandbox. Carlos — can you flip to the Console?
[00:03:05] Carlos Rivera: Sure. In Console -> Teams -> API Keys you can create scoped keys limited to models or routes. We recommend creating a "ci/smoke" key for CI and a separate "service" key for production. Also use RBAC to limit who can create keys.
[00:03:20] Priya Nair: Does Console expose audit logs for key creation and use?
[00:03:24] Carlos Rivera: Yes — audit logs and per-token usage breakdown. That helps for SOC2 evidence and for troubleshooting token leak incidents.

[00:03:34] Evan Shaw: On the topic of SOC2/compliance, can you share the compliance pack and SOC2 report?
[00:03:39] Maya Chen: Absolutely. We'll share the compliance bundle. For Private deployments we support customer-managed logging and SIEM integration too.

[00:03:49] [00:03:49] -- Architecture & Deploy choices --
[00:03:51] Carlos Rivera: Quick note on deployment modes: Hosted (fastest, us-west/eur regions), Dedicated (reserved GPUs for steady throughput + SLA), Private (VPC or on-prem for strict data residency). For PII/regulatory, most enterprises pick Dedicated or Private.
[00:04:07] Priya Nair: We likely need VPC access due to banking data. How does initial testing work?
[00:04:12] Maya Chen: You can do an early sandbox PoC on Hosted while we kick off a Dedicated/VPC provisioning — the sandbox is representative for API surface and functional tests; performance numbers will vary. We'll plan a later perf benchmark in your VPC.

[00:04:26] [00:04:26] -- Optimize: batching & KV cache --
[00:04:28] Carlos Rivera: Now Optimize: for throughput/cost you can tune batching and KV cache settings. For chat-like workloads the KV cache for long contexts avoids re-tokenizing prefixes. For short single-turn workloads, batching is the main lever.
[00:04:41] Jordan Miles: Any default batch sizes? We expect many short calls, like 150-200 tokens.
[00:04:46] Carlos Rivera: Default adaptive batching tries to keep latency SLOs; you can set max batch size and max latency window. We'll recommend starting with max batch=16 and a 40ms batch window for your traffic profile, then iterate.
[00:04:58] Priya Nair: You mentioned quantized variants earlier — will quality differ?
[00:05:01] Carlos Rivera: Slightly. Quantized models reduce cost but can change small answer differences. Redwood Optimize suggests quantization profiles per workload; we'll run a short eval on your prompt-set.

[00:05:15] [00:05:15] -- Security specifics --
[00:05:17] Maya Chen: For KMS and encryption: hosted accounts encrypt keys at rest and in transit; Dedicated/Private supports customer-managed KMS keys (AWS KMS, GCP KMS) and optionally HSM for higher assurance. Also SSO via SAML/OIDC and RBAC for tenant isolation.
[00:05:32] Evan Shaw: For audit requirements, do logs include per-request metadata? We need request IDs, timestamps, and deploy versions.
[00:05:39] Carlos Rivera: Yes, trace ids, model version, route, and timestamps are available, and can be exported to your ELK/Splunk.

[00:05:49] [00:05:49] -- Questions from BridgeLane --
[00:05:51] Priya Nair: If we hit a model regression after upgrading — can we rollback?
[00:05:55] Maya Chen: Yes, Console supports rollouts and automatic fallback policies to previous pinned versions. Also you can run canary fleets and compare outputs against evaluations in Optimize.
[00:06:04] Jordan Miles: For the POC, can you provide a minimal Terraform or CloudFormation for network setup?
[00:06:09] Carlos Rivera: We have example VPC peering and routing templates — we'll attach them. They include NAT, security groups, and routing rules for Dedicated and Private.

[00:06:20] [00:06:20] -- Live Quickstart walk-through --
[00:06:22] Carlos Rivera: I'm running the smoke test using the python SDK: client = RedwoodClient(api_key=os.getenv("REDWOOD_API_KEY")) response = client.generate(...). It returns tokens with streaming option.
[00:06:35] Priya Nair: The streaming option — can we stream to websocket or do we need to handle chunking?
[00:06:41] Carlos Rivera: We support server-sent events (SSE) and websockets for low-latency streaming. In TS the SDK wraps SSE by default.
[00:06:50] Evan Shaw: Any quotas we should be aware of during sandbox?
[00:06:54] Maya Chen: Sandbox has soft quotas; we'll increase them for the PoC as needed. For Dedicated we'll set the committed capacity in the contract.

[00:07:03] [00:07:03] -- Minor transcription artifacts / clarifications --
[00:07:05] Carlos Rivera: Sorry folks, sometimes the recorded docs call our "KV cache" as "kay-vee cache" in older notes — same thing. Also the product name in code examples is sometimes shortened to "redwood".
[00:07:20] Jordan Miles: No problem.

[00:07:22] -- Recap & Next Steps --
[00:07:24] Maya Chen: Quick recap: we'll send a sandbox invite + repo with python and TS quickstarts, a sample GitHub Actions CI workflow for key rotation, the SOC2/compliance bundle, and VPC templates. We'll also draft a short Optimize-run plan to evaluate batching/quantization with your prompt set.
[00:07:38] Priya Nair: Sounds great. Can you also include a sample eval harness for prompt regression checks?
[00:07:42] Carlos Rivera: Yes — small pytest-based harness we use for regressions.
[00:07:46] Evan Shaw: Timeline-wise, we want to start the PoC next week and have an initial perf run within 2 weeks.
[00:07:51] Maya Chen: We'll aim to have the sandbox and docs over by EOD Jun 4. POC scoping call — let's tentatively schedule Jun 10.
[00:07:59] Jordan Miles: Works for us.
[00:08:02] Maya Chen: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the artifacts.
[00:08:06] Priya Nair: Thanks, talk soon.

[00:08:10] -- End of recorded transcript excerpt (transcription contains minor errors and occasional mislabels; full recording available)
